Students will compare the novel's Oracle with the informational article on Delphi by identifying central ideas, supporting details, and technical vocabulary."},{"kind":"language","text":"Students will interpret figurative and symbolic phrasing in the prophecy and in the description of the Oracle, and use context and word parts to determine the meaning of unknown words. Answer the question on the board. Take turns, and give a reason for your answer."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"If someone could tell you one true thing about your future, would you want to hear it? Why or why not?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"I think I would want to know, because then I could get ready for hard things. But I'm also kind of scared, because if it was bad news I couldn't forget it."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Wanting to know the future and being afraid of it often go together. Today Percy meets the Oracle, and we will look at what her words show about what people hope for and what they fear."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Keep this to about 3 minutes of talk and 2 minutes of sharing. Write each word on the board and have students pronounce it chorally before analyzing it. Keep a quick pace: about one minute per word."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Let's start with *retreated*. Circle the prefix *re-*, which means 'back' or 'again.' Underline the root *treat*, from a Latin word meaning 'to draw or pull.' Circle the suffix *-ed*, which tells us it already happened. So *retreated* means 'pulled back.' When the spirit retreated on page 142, it pulled back after speaking."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Look at *confront*. The prefix *con-* means 'together' or 'with,' and the root *front* is the same as the front of your body. What do you think *confront* means?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"It means to stand front to front with something, like looking right at a problem or person instead of hiding from it."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"*Summoned* and *betrayed* both have word parts we can use. In *summoned* the beginning *sum-* comes from a Latin prefix meaning 'under,' and the root comes from a word for 'warn' or 'remind.' In *betrayed*, *be-* is a prefix and the root comes from a Latin word meaning 'hand over.' Using the parts and the sentence on the page, what does each word mean?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Summoned means called to come, like someone with power is warning you to show up. Betrayed means handed over or let down by someone who was supposed to be on your side."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"*Memento* comes from a Latin word for 'remember,' and you can hear the same idea in *memory* and *memorial*. A memento is an object that helps you remember something. Notice that these two words, *memento* and *memory*, share a root, so knowing one helps you with the other."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Word-part histories here are simplified for Grade 6. If students notice that *summon* does not break cleanly into parts, that is a good observation. Tell them that some words have changed over time and that context is the backup strategy."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Use your edition's page numbers from the Outline to point students to the sentence where each word appears (memento p. 140, betrayed p. 141, retreated p. 142, summoned p. 144, confront p. 146)."}]},{"id":"lab-context-organizer","title":"Context Clues and the Unit Vocabulary Organizer","minutes":4,"standards":["L.6.4","L.6.6"],"routine":"Annotation","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Open your Unit Vocabulary graphic organizer. Add all ten words from today: memento, tendrils, betrayed, retreated, grudge, summoned, confront, shredded, shrieked and rival. For each of the five words we just analyzed, mark the prefix, root and suffix and write the meaning in your own words. For the other five, find the word on the page listed and underline the context clues that help you guess its meaning."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Look at *shredded* and *shrieked* on pages 146–147. What do these two words tell you about the mood of the scene? What clues in the sentence helped you?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"They make the scene sound violent and scary. Shredded means torn into pieces and shrieked is a loud, high scream, so the author wants us to feel the danger."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"*Rival* and *grudge* are about relationships. What do they suggest about how characters in this chapter feel about each other?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"They suggest some characters are enemies who compete or stay angry for a long time. A grudge means someone is still mad about the past."},{"type":"pulse-check","standards":["L.6.4"],"stem":"A student reads that a character 'retreated' from a dangerous spirit. Using the prefix re- and the root treat (to pull), what does retreated most likely mean?","choices":[{"text":"Pulled back or moved away","correct":true,"rationale":"Correct. Re- means 'back' and treat means 'pull,' so retreated means pulled back, which fits a character moving away from danger."},{"text":"Looked at again more carefully","correct":false,"rationale":"This confuses re- meaning 'again' with the idea of looking, but the root treat has nothing to do with seeing or studying."},{"type":"x","text":"Walked forward to face the danger","correct":false,"rationale":"This is the opposite meaning. Confront means to face something, but retreated means to move back."},{"text":"Gave a gift to someone","correct":false,"rationale":"This confuses retreated with the word treat meaning a gift or snack, which is a different meaning of the spelling."}]},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: using word parts to infer meaning","tryThis":"Give students a three-box card (prefix, root, suffix) and one word at a time. Say the word aloud together, point to each part, then reread the sentence and ask whether the guess fits. Use the frame: I think ___ means ___ because the part ___ means ___."},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Ask students to find two other words with the prefix re- or con- from earlier chapters or other classes and explain how the prefix changes the meaning of the root."}]}]}]},{"kind":"learning-in-action","title":"Learning in Action","purpose":"Students analyze the Oracle scene closely for stated and implied meaning, figurative language and structure, then compare it with an informational article on Delphi and write an explanation using cohesive devices.","activities":[{"id":"lia-cite-prophecy","title":"Stated and Implied: The Prophecy and Percy's Reactions","minutes":8,"standards":["RL.6.1","RL.6.4","RL.6.3"],"routine":"Close Read & Annotation Protocol","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief, Chapter 9","pages":"pp. 139–148"},{"type":"directions","text":"Reread the part of Chapter 9 where the Oracle speaks the prophecy and Percy reacts. Make a two-column chart. In the left column, copy lines from the prophecy or from Percy's reactions. In the right column, write what the line says directly (stated) and what it suggests but does not say (implied)."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Let me model with one line. The prophecy says, 'You shall be betrayed by one who calls you a friend.' What is stated? That someone who says they are Percy's friend will betray him. What is implied? That Percy cannot be sure who he can trust, and that the person might be hiding their true feelings."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Choose a different line of the prophecy. What does it state, and what does it imply about Percy's future or the quest?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The line 'You shall go west, and face the god who has turned' states that Percy will travel west and face a god. It implies that a god has done something wrong or gone bad, and that Percy's quest is more dangerous than a normal camp game."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How does Percy react to the prophecy? Which words or actions on pages 139–148 show how he feels?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"On the page where the Oracle finishes speaking, Percy seems shaken and confused. His reaction shows he does not feel ready, which implies he is worried about whether he can handle the quest and who he can trust."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"The prophecy is four lines. Students should copy short, exact quotations and put quotation marks around them. If your edition's wording of the prophecy differs, use your copy. Select one or two of Percy's reactions from pp. 139–148 for students who need a starting point."},{"type":"pulse-check","standards":["RL.6.1"],"stem":"Which statement best shows an inference, not just a stated fact, about the line 'You shall be betrayed by one who calls you a friend'?","choices":[{"text":"Percy cannot be sure who is really loyal to him.","correct":true,"rationale":"Correct. The line does not say this directly, but it suggests Percy will have to doubt people who seem friendly."},{"text":"Someone will betray Percy.","correct":false,"rationale":"This is nearly a restatement of the line, so it is explicit rather than an inference."},{"text":"Percy will go to the west to fight a god.","correct":false,"rationale":"This comes from a different line of the prophecy, so it does not answer the question about the betrayal line."},{"text":"Percy's friends are all untrustworthy.","correct":false,"rationale":"This goes too far. The line says only one person, not all friends."}]},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support students in distinguishing explicit meaning from inference using precise reading language and present-tense verbs for literary analysis.","sayAsk":"Say: When we analyze a text, we use the simple present: The prophecy states..., Percy feels..., this implies... Ask: What does the line say directly? What does it suggest? Frames: The prophecy states that ___. This implies that ___ because ___. Percy's reaction shows that he feels ___.","watchFor":"If students retell the plot instead of analyzing, then prompt: 'Which exact words did you use as evidence?' If students mix past and present tense, then model the correction ('The prophecy states...') and have them repeat. Success: students quote a line accurately and write one stated and one implied meaning using present-tense verbs."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: telling stated from implied","tryThis":"Give two sentence starters, 'The text says...' and 'This makes me think...', and have students complete both for one line. Pair them with a partner to compare."},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Ask students to explain how two lines of the prophecy might work together to create a warning about the quest, using evidence from both lines."}]}]},{"id":"lia-figurative-language","title":"Interpreting the Oracle's Imagery","minutes":6,"standards":["L.6.5.a","L.6.4","RL.6.4"],"routine":"Annotation","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief, Chapter 9","pages":"pp. 139–145"},{"type":"directions","text":"Find at least two figurative or symbolic phrases in the description of the Oracle (for example, the green mist and its tendrils) or in the prophecy. Copy each phrase, explain what it literally means, and then explain what it suggests in context."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"A figure of speech uses words in a non-literal way to create a feeling or a picture. When the mist has *tendrils*, the author compares it to a plant that reaches out. That makes the mist seem alive, a kind of personification. It also makes it seem creeping and a little threatening."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Choose one phrase from the Oracle's description or the prophecy. What does it mean literally, and what does it suggest in context?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Literally, the mist has thin curling parts. In context, it suggests that the Oracle's power is alive and reaching toward Percy, which makes the scene feel eerie and dangerous."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"The prophecy says 'what matters most.' Why do you think Riordan leaves it unspecific?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"It leaves it open so readers and Percy have to wonder what he might lose. That suggests the future is scary because the most important thing could be anything."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Accept any reasonable reading of 'what matters most' that is tied to text evidence. The point is interpreting figurative language in context, not finding one right answer."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Help students read closely and evaluate how word choices create meaning, using verbs that describe effect.","sayAsk":"Say: Writers choose words to create a feeling. Ask: Which word creates the feeling of danger? Frames: The phrase ___ means ___ literally. In context, it suggests ___. The author uses the word ___ to make the scene feel ___.","watchFor":"If students give only a literal meaning, then prompt: 'What picture or feeling does this make? Why would the author want that?' If students struggle to name the feeling, then offer a word bank (eerie, threatening, mysterious, calm). Success: students give both literal and contextual meanings and name the effect on the reader."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: figurative language","tryThis":"Draw the phrase as a quick sketch (mist with curling tendrils), then write a caption explaining what the picture suggests about the Oracle."},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Ask students to rewrite the prophecy line using literal language, then explain what is lost when the figurative language is removed."}]}]},{"id":"lia-structural-hinge","title":"The Prophecy as a Structural Hinge","minutes":5,"standards":["RL.6.5","RL.6.3"],"routine":"Think-Pair-Share","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief, Chapter 9","pages":"pp. 139–148"},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"A hinge lets a door swing from one position to another. In a story, a hinge scene swings the plot in a new direction. Before Chapter 9, Percy is living and training at camp. After the prophecy, he is officially on a quest."},{"type":"directions","text":"Think for one minute, then share with a partner. Describe what Percy's life looks like at the start of the chapter, what changes after the Oracle speaks, and one later event the prophecy might shape."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How does this scene change the direction of the story? Use the words *before*, *after* and *consequently* in your answer."},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Before the prophecy, Percy is training and learning about the camp. After it, he has an official quest to find the lightning bolt. Consequently, the plot changes from camp life to a journey, and the warnings in the prophecy will shape what happens on the way."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Do not spoil later chapters. Students can predict how the prophecy might shape later events based on the lines (the west, the stolen item, the betrayal, the loss) without knowing what happens."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support students in explaining sequence and cause-effect using verbs and transition words.","sayAsk":"Say: Use before and after to show change. Ask: What changes after the Oracle speaks? Frames: Before the prophecy, Percy ___. After the prophecy, he ___. Consequently, the plot ___.","watchFor":"If students list events without showing change, then prompt: 'What is different for Percy after this scene?' Success: students use before/after and a cohesive device to explain the shift."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: structure","tryThis":"Give a simple two-box organizer labeled 'Before the prophecy' and 'After the prophecy' and have students fill in one detail for each."},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Ask students to predict how one line in the prophecy could create tension in a later chapter and explain what in Chapter 9 supports their prediction."}]}]},{"id":"lia-compare-article","title":"The Oracle in the Novel and the Oracle in the Article","minutes":7,"standards":["RL.6.9","RI.6.2","RI.6.4"],"routine":"Compare and Contrast Organizer","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"Delphi – Kids (Britannica Kids) or similar short article","pages":"Full article"},{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief, Chapter 9","pages":"pp. 139–148"},{"type":"directions","text":"Read the article on Delphi and the Oracle of Apollo. Use a two-column chart labeled 'Novel (Chapter 9)' and 'Article (Delphi)'. For each text, record the central idea, two supporting details, and any technical vocabulary (such as oracle, sanctuary, prophecy). Then write one similarity and one difference in how the texts present the Oracle."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"A central idea is the main point of a text. In an informational article, the central idea is supported by facts and details. In a novel, we can look for the larger idea a scene develops. The article is trying to inform. The novel is trying to tell a story and create suspense."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What is the central idea of the article? Which details support it?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The central idea is that Delphi was an important place in ancient Greece where people came to ask the Oracle of Apollo about the future. Supporting details include that people traveled there to ask questions and that a priestess spoke for the god."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How does the novel present the Oracle differently from the article?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The article gives facts about a real place and real people who believed in the Oracle. The novel turns the Oracle into a spooky character with green mist whose prophecy begins a quest. The article informs, but the novel builds suspense and fear."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What do both texts suggest about why people go to an oracle?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Both suggest people want to know what is coming so they can prepare. The article shows people traveling to ask, and in the novel Percy and the camp need guidance. That reflects how much people value knowing the future, and the scary prophecy shows they also fear it."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Article wording varies by version, so use the details in the article your students read. If you cannot access Britannica Kids, any short, student-friendly article on Delphi will work. Make sure students record technical vocabulary exactly as it appears."},{"type":"pulse-check","standards":["RL.6.9"],"stem":"Which statement best describes a difference in how the article and the novel present the Oracle?","choices":[{"text":"The article gives facts about a real place and its beliefs, while the novel makes the Oracle a mysterious character who launches a quest.","correct":true,"rationale":"Correct. This captures the difference in purpose and approach: informing versus telling a story with suspense."},{"text":"The article is about a different Oracle than the novel.","correct":false,"rationale":"Both texts are about the Oracle of Apollo, though they present it differently."},{"text":"The novel gives more facts about Delphi than the article.","correct":false,"rationale":"The article is the source of factual information. The novel uses the Oracle for plot and mood."},{"text":"The article and the novel present the Oracle in exactly the same way.","correct":false,"rationale":"They share a figure but differ in purpose, tone and details."}]},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support students in comparing two texts and using technical vocabulary and precise language.","sayAsk":"Say: When we compare, we look at how the texts are alike and different. Ask: How does each text present the Oracle? Frames: The article presents the Oracle as ___, but the novel presents the Oracle as ___. Both texts show that ___. The word ___ is technical vocabulary because ___.","watchFor":"If students list details without comparing, then prompt: 'Which detail in the article matches or differs from one in the novel?' If students struggle with technical words, then pair the word with a picture or a home-language cognate where possible (oráculo, profecía). Success: students identify a similarity and difference with evidence from both texts."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: comparing across forms","tryThis":"Offer a sentence frame for each box and have students complete the 'Article' column first, since it is more straightforward, then the 'Novel' column."},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Ask students to explain why Riordan might change facts about the Oracle for his story, and what the change helps him accomplish."}]}]},{"id":"lia-cohesive-writing","title":"Explain It: Connecting Evidence to Claims","minutes":4,"standards":["RL.6.9","RL.6.1","L.6.5.a"],"routine":"Quick Write","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Write 4–5 sentences that answer the question: How does the Oracle's prophecy reveal what people value and fear about the future? Use at least one quotation from Chapter 9, one detail from the article, and at least two of these cohesive devices: this suggests, this implies, this reflects, consequently, therefore."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Cohesive devices are signal words that show how your ideas connect. *This suggests* and *this implies* show you are interpreting evidence. *Consequently* and *therefore* show cause and effect. They help the reader follow your reasoning, not just your facts."},{"type":"paragraph","audience":"teacher","text":"Model paragraph (display if needed): The prophecy says Percy will be 'betrayed by one who calls you a friend.' This suggests that people fear being let down by those they trust most. In the article, people travel to Delphi to ask the Oracle about the future, which reflects how much they value knowing what is coming. Therefore, the novel and the article both show that people want guidance about the future but also fear what they might hear."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support students in writing a connected explanation using precise verbs and cohesive devices in the simple present.","sayAsk":"Say: In literary analysis, we use the simple present. Ask: What does the evidence suggest? Frames: The prophecy states ___. This suggests that ___. In the article, ___, which reflects ___. Consequently, ___.","watchFor":"If students write a list of facts, then prompt: 'Add a sentence that begins with this suggests or this reflects.' If students shift to past tense, then circle the verb and have them rewrite it in the present. Success: students include a quotation, a detail from the article and at least two cohesive devices."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: writing connected explanations","tryThis":"Provide a paragraph frame with blanks for quotation, interpretation and article detail. Allow students to say each sentence aloud to a partner before writing it."},{"type":"situation-extension","situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Ask students to add a final sentence that explains what the comparison shows about why authors adapt ancient myths."}]}]}]},{"kind":"look-back","title":"Look Back","purpose":"Students reflect on what the Oracle reveals about people's values and fears and how comparing texts deepens their understanding.","activities":[{"id":"look-back-exit-ticket","title":"Exit Ticket: What the Oracle Reveals","minutes":5,"standards":["RL.6.9","L.6.5.a"],"routine":"Reflection","blocks":[{"type":"paragraph","audience":"shared","text":"In the Performance Task, you will compare a fictional scene with an informational source. Today you practiced that by comparing Riordan's Oracle with the article on Delphi."},{"type":"directions","text":"Complete the paragraph: In Chapter 9, the Oracle's prophecy reveals that people value ___ and fear ___. The line '___' shows this because ___. Compared with the article on Delphi, the novel ___."},{"type":"sample-response","text":"In Chapter 9, the Oracle's prophecy reveals that people value knowing the future and fear losing what matters most. The line 'you shall fail to save what matters most, in the end' shows this because it warns Percy of a painful loss. Compared with the article on Delphi, the novel turns the Oracle into a scary character who launches a quest, while the article explains why real people visited her."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Collect the exit tickets and sort them into three piles (strong evidence, needs more evidence, unclear comparison) to guide small-group work in the next Flex Day."}]}]},{"kind":"homework","title":"Homework (Optional)","purpose":"Students prepare for Lesson 17 by reading the summary and annotating Chapter 10.","activities":[{"id":"homework-ch10","title":"Read and Annotate Chapter 10","minutes":0,"standards":["RL.6.10"],"routine":"Annotation","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Read the summary of Chapter 10 (pp. 149–157). Then read and annotate Chapter 10 of The Lightning Thief (pp. 158–167). As you read, mark one place where Percy faces danger and one place that shows a choice he makes."},{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief, Chapter 10","pages":"pp. 149–157 (summary) and pp. 158–167"}]}]}]},"digest":{"summary":"Students closely read the Oracle scene in Chapter 9 (pp. 139–148), analyzing stated and implied meaning in the prophecy and Percy's reactions, interpreting figurative language, and explaining the scene as a structural hinge into the quest. They then compare the novel's Oracle with an informational article on Delphi and write a connected explanation using cohesive devices.","keyActivities":["Morphology analysis of retreated, confront, summoned, betrayed and memento","Stated vs. implied chart for the prophecy and Percy's reactions","Interpreting the green mist and tendrils imagery","Before/after analysis of the prophecy as a structural hinge","Novel vs. Delphi article comparison chart","Quick Write with cohesive devices (this suggests, this reflects, consequently, therefore)"],"vocabularyTaught":["memento","tendrils","betrayed","retreated","grudge","summoned","confront","shredded","shrieked","rival"],"standardsCovered":["RL.6.9","L.6.4","L.6.5.a","RL.6.1","RL.6.3","RL.6.4","RL.6.5","RI.6.2","RI.6.4","L.6.6","RL.6.10"]}}
